text: As stated before, these findings can have profound potential implications for both applied fields and fundamental science. In vision science, the perception of overall naturalness in images remain a highly active yet unresolved research area. The present study provides an account of a potential cue used by the human visual system to judge the naturalness or plausibility of an image. In applied fields, the same framework offers practical utility for 3D rendering pipelines, where predicting when an object will appear excessively bright or unintentionally self-luminous could be helpful for achieving realistic tone mapping, material appearance, and physically based rendering. More specifically, in Augmented Reality (AR) and Mixed Reality (MR), where virtual objects must be seamlessly integrated into the real world, the ultimate goal is to create a perceptually convincing illusion in which users cannot reliably distinguish virtual content from real objects. A central challenge in achieving this level of realism is matching the illumination of virtual content to that of the surrounding environment, thereby preventing virtual objects from appearing self-luminous or perceptually “out of place” in either color or luminance. The physical gamut and luminosity threshold framework demonstrated in this study provides guidelines and quantitative boundaries that virtual objects should not exceed in order to maintain perceptual realism in AR/MR scenes. A similar principle applies to projection mapping, where controlling displayed luminance within the limits defined by the physical gamut can prevent projected surfaces from appearing emissive and thereby ensure a coherent and realistic integration with the real-world environment.
source_label: Optimal colors can predict luminosity thresholds in natural scenes
